brief-4-cost-of-being-uncertified.claim: Before 24 February 2026, being uncertified to a heavy-metals standard was a marketing question. After that date it is a balance-sheet question — and the cost sits in five places at once, which is why almost no brand has written it down.

after-palmquist.claim: A manufacturer won a heavy-metal case at trial, and the win was erased — not on the science, but on the courthouse. After Palmquist these cases are tried before state juries, with the retailer anchored in the room.

brief-2-open-category.claim: The heavy-metals category will be owned the way non-GMO was — by whoever plants the word and the picture first. Right now the word is unclaimed, the visual is empty, and the demand is already standing in the aisle.

brief-3-what-organic-doesnt-say.claim: Organic certifies how food is grown; it was never built to measure the metals that rise out of the soil. The honest response is not to replace the seal but to add the instrument that does the new job.

brief-5-retailer-as-anchor.claim: Palmquist turned the retailer from a peripheral defendant into a permanent one. Supplier qualification against a published standard is the operating response — and the retailer that writes it first sets the requirement for the category.

brief-6-premium-promise.claim: A premium brand sells trust, its most valuable and most fragile asset. After Palmquist the brands with the most to lose are the ones whose promise is still unproven — and they are the last to believe it.

brief-7-four-vs-eight.claim: The regulators moved to eight metals. A certificate that stayed at four certifies the past — and hands the brands wearing it a blind spot they pay for without being told it is there.

brief-8-surveillance-protocol.claim: Two certifications can carry the same mark and mean opposite things in a deposition. One is a photograph; the other is a record — and which one a brand holds is settled years before any complaint is filed.

defense-counsel-briefing.claim: The contested ground has moved from whether the plaintiff’s science comes in to what each side’s own documented record shows — and the record that decides a post-Palmquist state-court trial is built before the complaint, or it is not built at all.

hmtc-primer.claim: This is a complete and neutral description of the program — what it certifies, what a licensee signs, and, with equal care, what it does not claim and where its conflicts lie. Nothing here should be a surprise later.

supplements-child-protective.claim: HMTc applies selected infant-food contaminant benchmarks to supplements as voluntary criteria. The comparison must state the product and exposure basis; meeting those criteria does not establish that an adult supplement is suitable for a child.

the-mucosal-gap.claim: Menstrual and intimate-care products contact the vaginal mucosa, more permeable than skin, for hours at a time. Lead, cadmium, and arsenic have been measured in tampons across brands and markets, and no government requires their metal content to meet a limit before sale. HMTc tests every lot to a limit built for the exposure route, and certifies heavy-metal safety: nothing else.

first-feminine-care-standard.claim: No government requires a menstrual device to meet a heavy-metal content limit before it is sold, and the voluntary numbers that exist do not bind every product. HMTc holds the full analyte panel to per-analyte ceilings, each read across from the strictest mucosal-contact health limit a government has drawn, and verifies them on every production lot.
